parole.significato: A saddle blanket.
parole.testo: From an Algonquian language term for "something to sit on". Compare Cree ᐊᐢᐹᐏᑲᓀᐦᐃᑲᐣ (aspaawikanehikan, “saddle blanket”) and Ojibwe apishimon/apishamon (“something to lie down upon”).

parole.significato: The pawpaw (Asimina triloba), a fruit-bearing plant.
parole.testo: From an Algonquian word *assimin or *rassimin (the second element of which is -min, "berry, fruit"), via Cajun French assiminier.

parole.significato: A member of an Ojibwe people of central North America, the Manitoba Saulteaux.
parole.testo: 1776 sense of people, 1951 language. From Algonquian, compare Cree ᐸᐦᑭ (pahki, “part, thing, a little”), Ojibwe bangii (“part, thing, a little”)/ᐸᓐᑶ.

parole.significato: A social gathering, usually for dancing.
parole.testo: From an Algonquian (probably Lenape) language; compare Unami këntke (“he dances”) and English cantico.

parole.significato: A usually preliminary meeting of party members to nominate candidates for public office or delegates to be sent to a no…
parole.testo: Unknown. Often claimed to be from an Algonquian language; transcribed words such as cawaassough and caucauasu meaning "counselor, elder, adviser" appear in early texts. A popular folk etymology attested in Great Leaders and National Issues of 1896 stated: "In the early part of the eighteenth century

parole.testo: Like its cognate / alternative form chinkapin, chinquapin is an alteration of chechinquamin / chincomen (the form found in early records), from an Algonquian language (sometimes said specifically to be from Powhatan). The final element is *mini (“berry, fruit”). Hewitt suggested that the first eleme

parole.significato: A conner, a fish of species Tautogolabrus adspersus.
parole.testo: Shortening of cachogset, from an Algonquian language; probably Mohegan-Pequot cachauxet (“conner”).

parole.significato: Symphyotrichum puniceum, red-stemmed aster, the roots of which were formerly used medicinally.
parole.testo: Of Algonquian origin, related to Massachusett kushki (“(it is) rough”), as many parts of the plant are rough. Compare cohosh, of similar origin.

parole.significato: A perennial American herb (Caulophyllum thalictroides), the rough rootstock of which is used in medicine.
parole.testo: From an Algonquian word meaning rough, probably from Eastern Abenaki / Penobscot *kkwὰhas. Compare Massachusett kushki (“(it is) rough”). Compare English cocash.

parole.significato: A viburnum of species Viburnum acerifolium, native to eastern North America.
parole.testo: From Algonquian, perhaps from Lenape dogekumak (“an unknown smokable plant”) via Dutch (whence the diminutive ending -ie), or perhaps from a Mahican word.

parole.significato: Any of the Native Americans of the Nottoway, Meherrin and Tuscarora groups.
parole.testo: From Algonquian.

parole.significato: The soft-shell clam.
parole.testo: From a Native American language of the Carolinas, probably an Algonquian one, thus probably from Carolina Algonquian.

parole.significato: A type of mantle made from fur, worn by some Native Americans.
parole.testo: Anglicized version of an Algonquian word — compare Ojibwe majigoodenh (“dress”) — with the spelling altered under the influence of the English words match and coat.

parole.significato: A box-like container made from birch-bark, especially one in which sugar is stored.
parole.testo: From an Algonquian language, probably Ojibwe makak (“semi-rigid container, birch bark basket, box”).

parole.significato: A semiaquatic rodent of the tribe Ondatrini.
parole.testo: Perhaps so called for its musky odour and because it resembles a rat, or perhaps called by an Algonquian name like the Abenaki moskwas, with the spelling altered under the influence of the English words musk and rat.

parole.significato: Indian corn parched and pounded into meal (powder), used as food by Native Americans, sometimes mixed with maple sugar.
parole.testo: A respelling, probably influenced by cake, of nokehick, nokehike, which derives from an Algonquian language, probably Narragansett nokehick or Massachusett nookhik (“nocake”, literally “(that which is) pounded till soft”); the word is related to Abenaki nokhigan (“flour”), and English rokeag and yok

parole.significato: A ceremonial war axe, the tomahawk throwing axe, which functions as a tobacco smoking pipe, with the bowl located on th…
parole.testo: By surface analysis, pipe (“pipe for smoking”) + tomahawk.

parole.significato: A (member of a) Native American tribe, the Fall River Wampanoag.
parole.testo: From Algonquian.

parole.significato: A low, wooded swamp in (especially coastal) Eastern Maryland, Virginia or the Carolinas; a palustrine wetland with deep…
parole.testo: From an unknown Algonquian word, sometimes suggested to be one meaning "opening out" (the widening of a river, related to Ojibwe baakisin (“it is left open”)), or "swamp on a hill". Alternatively, perhaps related to Abenaki pôgwaso (“very shallow”).

parole.significato: A marsh; an area of grassy ground partly covered with (generally stagnant) water adjacent or connected to a stream or l…
parole.testo: Uncertain. Often suggested to be from an Algonquian language. Perhaps related to pocosin. Early spellings like Pokee Login and Pocologan (found especially in place names) suggest the four-syllable pronunciation is older.

parole.significato: A low box-like sleigh designed to be pulled by one horse.
parole.testo: Shortened form of tom-pung, from the same Algonquian etymon as toboggan.

parole.significato: A prefabricated building having a roof of corrugated iron and semicircular cross section.
parole.testo: Named after Quonset Point, the place they were manufactured; the placename derives from an Algonquian language.

parole.significato: A lightweight prefabricated structure of corrugated galvanized steel, having a semicircular cross section.
parole.testo: Named after Quonset Point, the place they were manufactured; the placename derives from an Algonquian language.

parole.significato: Synonym of sachem.
parole.testo: From an Algonquian language; compare Abenaki sôgmô, sôgemô (“chief”), Mi'kmaq saqamaw (“chief”), and Penobscot sagama, sagema, sagemo, sangemo (“chief”), all ultimately from Proto-Algonquian *sa·kima·wa (“male chief”). Doublet of sachem.

parole.significato: A large greenish-bronze grape native to the Southeastern United States, a variety of the muscadine grape (Vitis rotundi…
parole.testo: Named after the Scuppernong River and Lake in North Carolina near which the grapes were first found and cultivated. Probably from an Algonquian word. Both senses, "grape" and "wine", are first found in documents from the 1800s-1820s.

parole.significato: A pokeberry or pokeweed plant (Phytolacca americana) or its dark red or purple fruit.
parole.testo: Perhaps a half-translation of an Algonquian term for "red berry" (compare Abenaki mkw-, mskw- (“red”)), in reference to the berries' red colour. Alternatively, perhaps a half-translation of an Algonquian term such as Penobscot *skokimin (“snake berry”), in reference to the fact that the plant is poi

parole.significato: Dark-coloured shell-money, used by Native Americans.
parole.testo: Of Native American origin, probably Algonquian, origin. Roger Williams writes that "suck-" signifies "black"; compare Unami sëk- (“black”).

parole.significato: A porridge made from cornmeal, similar to polenta; hasty pudding; mush.
parole.testo: Ultimately from an Algonquian language term such as Massachusett/Narragansett saupan (“softened by water”), Munsee nsá·pa·n, or a cognate thereof, whence also English samp. Possibly transmitted via New Netherland Dutch or Jersey Dutch suppaen, sapaen.

parole.significato: A member of a group of Iroquoian-speaking Native Americans who lived in areas adjacent to the Susquehanna River and its…
parole.testo: Of Algonquian origin, said to mean "people of the muddy river."

parole.significato: A loggers' large raft with a shanty built on top for accommodation and cooking.
parole.testo: From an Algonquian language spoken in the Maine area. Compare wannigan.

parole.significato: Any of several trees, such as the leatherwood/moosewood (of the genus Dirca), the whitewood, or the American basswood/l…
parole.testo: From an Algonquian term for "stringy bark"; compare Abenaki wigebi (“stringy inner bark (used as cordage)”), Ojibwe wiigob (“inner bark of a basswood”).

parole.significato: The American wigeon.
parole.testo: Probably from an Algonquian language; compare Ojibwe zhiishiib (“duck”).

parole.significato: An edible clam with a hard shell found along the Atlantic Coast of North America, from species Mercenaria mercenaria, f…
parole.testo: Most often thought to be from Narragansett poquaûhock (“hard clam”), or perhaps from pohkeni (“dark”) + hogki (“shell”). Alternatively from Mohegan-Pequot p'quaghhaug (“hard clam”) or another Algonquian language.
